# 🌌 Welcome to the `tidyverse`

## What is the tidyverse?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="55%"}
::: {.incremental}
- A **collection of R packages** by Hadley Wickham, Mara Averick, and the team at Posit.
- All of them share the **same grammar**: data goes in, transformed data comes out.
- If you learn one, you basically know the others.
- It is the **modern way** to do data science in R.
:::
:::
::: {.column width="45%"}
![](img/wickham.png){fig-align="center" width="80%"}
:::
:::

---

## The packages you'll use most 📦

| Package | What it does |
|---------|-------------|
| [**`dplyr`**](https://dplyr.tidyverse.org/) | Wrangle data: filter, select, mutate, summarise |
| [**`tidyr`**](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/) | Reshape data: long ↔ wide, separate, unite |
| [**`ggplot2`**](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/) | Make plots |
| [**`readr`**](https://readr.tidyverse.org/) | Import data (csv, tsv) |
| [**`tibble`**](https://tibble.tidyverse.org/) | A nicer `data.frame` |
| [**`stringr`**](https://stringr.tidyverse.org/) | Work with text |
| [**`forcats`**](https://forcats.tidyverse.org/) | Work with categorical variables (factors) |
| [**`purrr`**](https://purrr.tidyverse.org/) | Functional programming (loops without loops) |

::: {.fragment}
**Loading them all at once:**

```r
library(tidyverse)
```
:::

---

## What is *tidy data*?

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.incremental}
A dataset is **tidy** when:

1. Each **variable** is a column.
2. Each **observation** is a row.
3. Each **value** is in its own cell.
:::

::: {.fragment}
> Tidy data makes every analysis 10× easier.
> Untidy data is where most of your time goes. 😩
:::
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](img/tidydata.png){fig-align="center"}
:::
:::

![](img/data-science-workflow.png){fig-align="center"}

::: {.fragment}
> 🧼 You'll spend **80% of your time here**. That's normal.
:::

## A word about *tibbles* 📋

A **tibble** is just a friendlier `data.frame`. When you load the tidyverse, almost every function returns a tibble.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`data.frame` (base R)**

- Prints *everything* (scary on big data)
- Auto-converts strings to factors (annoying)
- Partial matching — silent bugs
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`tibble` (tidyverse)**

- Prints only the first 10 rows + tells you the dimensions
- Never converts strings to factors automatically
- Tells you when you typo a column name
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
Don't overthink it — **a tibble is a data.frame with better manners**. You can use them interchangeably.
:::

# 🪈 The Pipe Operator

## What does the pipe do?

The pipe means **"and then"** — it takes whatever is on the left and feeds it as the *first argument* of the function on the right.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Without the pipe** 😵

```r
arrange(
  filter(
    select(starwars, name, height, mass),
    species == "Human"
  ),
  desc(height)
)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**With the pipe** 😎

```r
starwars |>
  select(name, height, mass) |>
  filter(species == "Human") |>
  arrange(desc(height))
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> Reads like a recipe: *"take starwars, **and then** select these columns, **and then** filter, **and then** arrange."*
:::

---

## Two pipes exist — use `|>` 🎯

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.incremental}
- **`|>`** — the **native** R pipe (since R 4.1, 2021). No package needed.
- **`%>%`** — the **classic** `magrittr` pipe (loaded by `library(tidyverse)`).
- They do **the same thing** for our purposes.
- **We'll use `|>` this week.** When you read older code or tutorials, you'll see `%>%` — same idea.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Keyboard shortcut for `|>`:**

- 🍎 Mac: `⌘ + ⇧ + M`
- 🪟 Windows / Linux: `Ctrl + Shift + M`

(In RStudio: *Tools → Global Options → Code → ✅ Use native pipe operator*)
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](img/pipe.png)

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-note}
## Fun fact
`%>%` lives in a package called **`magrittr`** — a tribute to René Magritte's painting *"The Treachery of Images"* (the famous *"Ceci n'est pas une pipe"*). 🎨
:::
:::
:::
:::

# 🛠️ The dplyr Verbs

## Why dplyr?

::: {.incremental}
- A **grammar of data manipulation**: a small set of *verbs* that do one thing well.
- Everything chains together with the pipe.
- Works the same on a tiny tibble *or* a million-row database.
:::

::: {.fragment}
**Today's verbs** 👇

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `count()`
- `arrange()`
- `filter()`
- `select()`
- `rename()`
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
- `mutate()` (+ `if_else`, `case_when`)
- `summarise()` (with `.by`)
- `*_join()` family
:::
:::
:::

---

## Verb syntax

All verbs follow the same shape:

> **`function(data, argument1, argument2, ...)`**

::: {.fragment}
But because we use the pipe, the data comes first:

> **`data |> function(argument1, argument2, ...)`**

The pipe automatically passes `data` as the first argument. ✨
:::

---

## Before we start: let's create a tibble we'll reuse

We'll calculate **BMI** for each character and call the result `starwars_bmi`.

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Base R 🤢**

```{r}
#| echo: true
starwars$bmi <- starwars$mass / (starwars$height / 100)^2
```

Lots of `$`, lots of repetition.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Tidyverse 😎**

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| code-line-numbers: "1|2|3|4"
starwars_bmi <-
    starwars |>
    mutate(bmi = mass / (height / 100)^2) |>
    select(bmi, everything())
```

Reads like English.
:::
:::

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi
```

# 🔢 `count()` — frequency tables

## Count values in a column

`count()` tells you **how many rows** there are per category. The most useful verb for exploring categorical data.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars |>
    count(species)
```

---

## `count()` with `sort = TRUE`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars |>
    count(species, sort = TRUE)
```

::: {.fragment}
> 🧠 Use this on every categorical variable when you start exploring a dataset. It's a 1-liner that catches data-entry errors and class imbalance instantly.
:::

# 🔃 `arrange()` — order rows

## Arrange ascending

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    arrange(bmi)
```

---

## Arrange descending with `desc()`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    arrange(desc(bmi))
```

# 🔍 `filter()` — pick rows

## Equal to

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    filter(sex == "female")
```

---

## Not equal to

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    filter(sex != "female")
```

---

## Numeric comparisons

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    filter(birth_year >= 112)
```

---

## Combine conditions

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    filter(sex == "male", height > 180) # AND
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    filter(sex == "male" | height > 180) # OR
```
:::

---

## ⚠️ NA gotcha

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
# This DROPS NAs silently:
starwars_bmi |> filter(sex == "male") |> nrow()
```

::: {.fragment}
```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
# To explicitly check for missing:
starwars_bmi |> filter(is.na(sex)) |> nrow()
```
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## `==` and `NA`
`NA == "male"` returns `NA`, **not** `FALSE`. So `filter(sex == "male")` drops missing rows. Always check missingness explicitly with `is.na()`.
:::
:::

---

## 🆕 `filter_out()` — drop rows the easy way

::: {.callout-note}
## New in dplyr 1.2.0 (Feb 2026)
`filter()` is *designed* for keeping rows. When you want to **drop** rows, use the new `filter_out()` — much clearer and safer with NAs.
:::

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The old way 😬**

```r
patients |> 
  filter(!(deceased & date < 2012))
```

Easy to write, easy to get wrong: this **drops `NA`s too**, which you usually don't want.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**The new way 😎**

```r
patients |> 
  filter_out(deceased, date < 2012)
```

Reads like Stata's `drop if`. NAs stay, which is usually what you want when *dropping*.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## When to reach for `filter_out()`
If you find yourself writing `!=`, `!`, or `!is.na()` to "drop" rows, that's your cue. `filter_out()` was made for exactly that. 📖 [Read more](https://tidyverse.org/blog/2026/02/dplyr-1-2-0/)
:::
:::

# ✂️ `select()` — pick columns

## Keep specific columns

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    select(name, bmi, sex)
```

---

## Drop columns with `-`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    select(-bmi)
```

---

## Chain it together

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    select(name, bmi, sex) |>
    filter(sex == "male") |>
    arrange(bmi)
```

# 🏷️ `rename()` — change column names

## Rename columns

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    select(name, bmi, sex) |>
    filter(sex == "male") |>
    arrange(bmi) |>
    rename(personaje = name, sexo = sex)
```

::: {.fragment}
**Pro tip**: you can rename *inside* `select()`:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    select(personaje = name, sexo = sex, bmi)
```
:::

# 💜 `mutate()` — create / modify columns

## My personal favorite

`mutate()` adds new variables that are **functions of existing variables**.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    mutate(id = row_number()) |>
    select(id, name, sex, bmi) |>
    filter(sex == "male") |>
    arrange(bmi)
```

---

## `mutate()` + `if_else()` — binary recodes

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars |>
    mutate(
        is_blue_eyes = if_else(eye_color == "blue", 1, 0, missing = NA_real_)
    ) |>
    select(name, eye_color, is_blue_eyes) |>
    arrange(desc(is_blue_eyes))
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Always set `missing = `
`if_else()` will return `NA` for missing inputs by default. Be explicit so you know what's happening.
:::
:::

---

## `mutate()` + `case_when()` — multi-way recodes 💜

`case_when()` lets you handle **many conditions** at once. Each condition is `condition ~ value`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars |>
    mutate(
        is_human = case_when(
            species == "Human" ~ 1,
            species != "Human" ~ 0,
            .default = NA
        )
    ) |>
    select(name, species, is_human)
```

---

## A more interesting `case_when()`

Categorize BMI into clinical groups:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    mutate(
        bmi_category = case_when(
            bmi < 18.5 ~ "Underweight",
            bmi >= 18.5 & bmi < 25 ~ "Normal weight",
            bmi >= 25 & bmi < 30 ~ "Overweight",
            bmi >= 30 & bmi < 35 ~ "Obesity Class I",
            bmi >= 35 & bmi < 40 ~ "Obesity Class II",
            bmi >= 40 ~ "Obesity Class III",
            .default = NA_character_
        )
    ) |>
    select(name, bmi, bmi_category)
```

::: {.fragment}
> 🌟 You'll use this exact pattern on **YRBS** to create risk categories.
:::

---

## 🆕 `recode_values()` — when you're matching values

::: {.callout-note}
## New in dplyr 1.2.0 (Feb 2026)
When every condition looks like `column == value ~ ...`, that's a sign you should use **`recode_values()`** instead. It removes the repetition.
:::

Recoding a Likert score into labels:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**With `case_when()` 😅**

```r
likert |> mutate(
  category = case_when(
    score == 1 ~ "Strongly disagree",
    score == 2 ~ "Disagree",
    score == 3 ~ "Neutral",
    score == 4 ~ "Agree",
    score == 5 ~ "Strongly agree"
  )
)
```

`score ==` repeated 5 times. 🙄
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**With `recode_values()` ✨**

```r
likert |> mutate(
  category = score |> recode_values(
    1 ~ "Strongly disagree",
    2 ~ "Disagree",
    3 ~ "Neutral",
    4 ~ "Agree",
    5 ~ "Strongly agree"
  )
)
```

Just the mapping. Clean. 💎
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Bonus: lookup tables
`recode_values()` also accepts `from = ` and `to = ` arguments, so your mapping can live in a separate tibble (or even a CSV) — perfect for long pipelines or shared reference data.
:::
:::

---

## 🆕 `replace_values()` — partial updates the easy way

For when you want to **fix a few values** in a column without touching the rest. Especially great for handling missingness.

```r
state <- c("NC", "NY", "CA", NA, "NY", "Unknown", NA)

# Replace NAs with a label
state |> replace_values(NA ~ "Unknown")
#> [1] "NC"  "NY"  "CA"  "Unknown" "NY" "Unknown" "Unknown"

# Treat "Unknown" as missing
state |> replace_values("Unknown" ~ NA)

# Standardize multiple problem values at once
state |> replace_values(c(NA, "Unknown") ~ "<missing>")
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-tip}
## Why this is great
Cleaner than `if_else(is.na(state), "Unknown", state)`, type-stable, and **pipe-friendly** (your column is the first argument). 💛

📖 [Full blog post on dplyr 1.2.0 →](https://tidyverse.org/blog/2026/02/dplyr-1-2-0/)
:::
:::

# 📊 `summarise()` — collapse rows

## *I always get it wrong the first time* 😒

`summarise()` reduces many rows down to **one row** (or one row per group).

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    summarise(
        mean_bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE)
    )
```

::: {.fragment}
::: {.callout-warning}
## Always `na.rm = TRUE`
By default, `mean(c(1, 2, NA))` returns `NA`. Use `na.rm = TRUE` so missing values are skipped.
:::
:::

---

## Summarise *by group* with `.by =`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi |>
    summarise(
        mean_bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_bmi = sd(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
        min = min(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
        max = max(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
        n = n(),
        .by = sex
    )
```

---

## `.by =` vs `group_by()` — same idea, two flavors

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Modern (`.by`):**

```r
starwars_bmi |>
  summarise(
    mean_bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
    .by = sex
  )
```

One step, no leftovers.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Classic (`group_by`):**

```r
starwars_bmi |>
  group_by(sex) |>
  summarise(
    mean_bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) |>
  ungroup()
```

You'll see this everywhere in older code.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> Both work. Pick one. The `.by` version is newer and slightly cleaner.
:::

---

## Building a summary step by step

**Step 1**: create the BMI categories and save as a new tibble:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi_cat <-
    starwars_bmi |>
    mutate(
        bmi_category = case_when(
            bmi < 18.5 ~ "Underweight",
            bmi >= 18.5 & bmi < 25 ~ "Normal weight",
            bmi >= 25 & bmi < 30 ~ "Overweight",
            bmi >= 30 & bmi < 35 ~ "Obesity Class I",
            bmi >= 35 & bmi < 40 ~ "Obesity Class II",
            bmi >= 40 ~ "Obesity Class III",
            .default = NA_character_
        )
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(bmi_category))

starwars_bmi_cat
```

::: {.callout-tip}
## The arrow `<-`
`object_name <- value` saves the result so you can reuse it. Shortcut: `Option/Alt + -`.
:::

---

## Step 2: summarize the saved object

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi_cat |>
    summarise(
        mean_bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_bmi = sd(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
        n = n(),
        .by = c(bmi_category, species)
    ) |>
    arrange(bmi_category, mean_bmi)
```

---

## Same idea — collapse "Human vs not"

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_bmi_cat |>
    mutate(
        is_human = if_else(species == "Human", "Human", "Other", missing = NA)
    ) |>
    filter(!is.na(is_human)) |>
    summarise(
        mean_bmi = mean(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
        sd_bmi = sd(bmi, na.rm = TRUE),
        n = n(),
        .by = c(bmi_category, is_human)
    ) |>
    arrange(bmi_category)
```

# 🤝 The `*_join()` Family

## When do you need a join?

When you have **two tables that share an ID** and want to combine them.

| Join | What it returns |
|------|-----------------|
| **`left_join(x, y)`** | All rows from `x`, matched rows from `y` |
| **`right_join(x, y)`** | All rows from `y`, matched rows from `x` |
| **`inner_join(x, y)`** | Only rows that match in **both** |
| **`full_join(x, y)`** | All rows from **either** |
| **`anti_join(x, y)`** | Rows in `x` *not* matched in `y` (great for QC) |

---

## A natural Star Wars example

Imagine the `starwars` data was split across two tables:

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`sw_basics`** — physical traits

```{r}
#| echo: true
sw_basics <- starwars |>
    select(name, height, mass)

sw_basics
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**`sw_origin`** — biographical info

```{r}
#| echo: true
sw_origin <- starwars |>
    select(name, species, homeworld) |>
    slice(1:60) # only first 60 characters

sw_origin
```
:::
:::

::: {.fragment}
> Notice: `sw_basics` has **87** characters, `sw_origin` has only **60**. What happens when we join them?
:::

---

## `left_join()` — keep everyone in the left table

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
sw_basics |>
    left_join(sw_origin, by = "name")
```

::: {.fragment}
> Characters not in `sw_origin` get `NA` for species and homeworld.
:::

---

## `inner_join()` — only matches in both

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
sw_basics |>
    inner_join(sw_origin, by = "name")
```

::: {.fragment}
> Drops anyone missing from either table.
:::

---

## `anti_join()` — find what's missing 🕵️

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
sw_basics |>
    anti_join(sw_origin, by = "name")
```

::: {.fragment}
> Use this for **quality control**: which IDs in your survey aren't in your roster?
:::

# 🔄 Reshaping: `tidyr`

## Long vs. wide data

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Wide format**

[One row per character — different attributes are different columns.]{.mark}

```{r}
#| echo: true
starwars |>
    select(name, height, mass, hair_color)
```
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Long format**

[One row per *attribute* — name + variable + value.]{.mark}

```{r}
#| echo: true
starwars |>
    select(name, height, mass, hair_color) |>
    mutate(across(-name, as.character)) |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -name,
        names_to = "attribute",
        values_to = "value"
    )
```
:::
:::

---

## Why does this matter? 🤔

::: {.incremental}
- **`ggplot2`** wants long data for plotting many series at once.
- **Many models** in `tidymodels` need long format.
- **Some tables** are easier to read in wide format.
- Knowing how to flip between them = a superpower. ✨
:::

---

## `pivot_longer()` — wide → long

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_long <-
    starwars |>
    select(name, height, mass, hair_color) |>
    mutate(across(-name, as.character)) |>
    pivot_longer(
        cols = -name,
        names_to = "attribute",
        values_to = "value"
    )

starwars_long
```

📖 [Documentation](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/pivot_longer.html)

---

## `pivot_wider()` — long → wide

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
starwars_long |>
    pivot_wider(
        names_from = attribute,
        values_from = value
    )
```

📖 [Documentation](https://tidyr.tidyverse.org/reference/pivot_wider.html)

# 📈 Bonus: A First Taste of `ggplot2`

## Anatomy of a ggplot

Three pieces:

1. **Data** — the tibble you want to plot
2. **Aesthetics** (`aes()`) — which columns map to x, y, color, size…
3. **Geoms** — the type of plot (`geom_point`, `geom_boxplot`, `geom_bar`…)

```r
ggplot(data, aes(x = ..., y = ...)) +
  geom_*()
```

::: {.callout-note}
## Notice: `+`, not `|>`
ggplot uses **`+`** to add layers, not the pipe. (One of those quirky things.)
:::

---

## A boxplot on Star Wars

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
starwars_bmi_cat |>
    filter_out(sex == "hermaphroditic") |>
    ggplot(aes(x = sex, y = bmi)) +
    geom_boxplot(aes(fill = sex), alpha = 0.6) +
    geom_jitter(width = 0.15, alpha = 0.5) +
    labs(
        x = NULL,
        y = "BMI",
        title = "BMI by sex in the Star Wars universe"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

---

## A bar chart of counts

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: column
starwars |>
    count(species, sort = TRUE) |>
    slice(1:10) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = n, y = fct_reorder(species, n))) +
    geom_col(fill = "steelblue") +
    labs(
        x = "Count",
        y = NULL,
        title = "Top 10 species in the Star Wars data"
    ) +
    theme_minimal()
```

::: {.fragment}
> `fct_reorder()` is from `forcats` — sorts the bars by count.
:::

# 🌍 Now: Land It On YRBS

## From Star Wars to your real project

You just learned the verbs. Now let's apply them to **the dataset for your project**: the YRBS data inside your `ml-template`.

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
library(tidyverse)
library(rio)

# Load the analysis data shipped with your template
analysis_data <- import("models/data/analysis_data.rds")

glimpse(analysis_data)
```

::: {.fragment}
> The verbs are **the same**. Only the data changes. ✨
:::

---

## Quick demo: `count()` an outcome variable

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
analysis_data |>
    count(SuicideIdeation, sort = TRUE)
```

```
# A tibble: 3 × 2
  SuicideIdeation     n
  <chr>           <int>
1 No               9215
2 Yes              1708
3 NA                  …
```

::: {.fragment}
> 🧠 *Right away* you see the **class imbalance** — that will matter on Wednesday when we train models.
:::

---

## `mutate()` + `case_when()` on YRBS

Build a "risk level" variable from a few binary indicators:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
analysis_data |>
    mutate(
        risk_level = case_when(
            GunCarrying == "Yes" | UnsafeAtSchool == "Yes" ~ "High",
            AttackedInNeighborhood == "Yes" ~ "Medium",
            .default = "Low"
        )
    ) |>
    count(risk_level)
```

::: {.fragment}
> Same `case_when()` you wrote for BMI — different domain. 💪
:::

---

## `summarise()` by group on YRBS

Mean age by suicide-ideation group:

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| eval: false
analysis_data |>
    filter(!is.na(SuicideIdeation)) |>
    summarise(
        mean_age = mean(Age, na.rm = TRUE),
        n = n(),
        .by = SuicideIdeation
    )
```
